catalog_quote: Stress in South Sulawesi languages usually occurs on the penultimate syllable. In such cases it is not marked in the word lists. Where stress deviates from the normal pattern or where stress may be unclear due to double vocoids, etc., it is marked with an apostrophe preceding the stressed syllable. [p. 94] ... Masenrempulu. The Enrekang dialect contrasts a back velar nasal [ŋ] with a normal velar nasal [ŋ]. Where the Enrekang dialect manifests [ŋ] many other South Sulawesi languages exhibit word-final [k] or glottal. For example: ['tasiŋ] sea, ['pusuŋ] nose, [manuŋmanuŋ] bird, ['tanduŋ] horn [p. 96; the backed velar nasal of the original is rendered here as plain ŋ]

new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress on the penultimate syllable, as the default for all South Sulawesi languages surveyed; the Enrekang (Masenrempulu-Enrekang) wordlist taken at Enrekang is transcribed under that convention, and the Enrekang examples in the areal note (['tasiŋ] 'sea', ['pusuŋ] 'nose', ['tanduŋ] 'horn') carry the stress mark on the penult. Only 5 of 51 MSR wordlist lines show an apostrophe (deviations or unclear cases, mostly vowel sequences).
new_statements.exceptions: Only the areal remark that stress may deviate from the normal pattern or be unclear with double vocoids (marked by apostrophe); the Selayar antepenult note is about Selayar, not Enrekang. Djunaidi 1993 (snippet only, not opened) states that Massenrempulu word stress is phonemic — shifting stress between syllables changes meaning — which for the sister dialect Duri (Valkama 1993) corresponds to suffixes moving stress to the new penult while enclitics do not.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, isolated citation forms in a survey wordlist. The rule is stated for the South Sulawesi family as a whole, not for Enrekang specifically; the Enrekang-specific evidence is the transcription of the Enrekang wordlist and three marked examples. No dedicated Enrekang phonology has been opened.
new_statements.identity_note: Enrekang = the Enrekang/Endekan dialect of the Massenrempulu cluster (Grimes & Grimes 1987 treat Maiwa, Enrekang and Duri as dialects of one 'Masenrempulu' language; Ethnologue/Glottolog split them: Duri duri1242, Maiwa (Indonesia) maiw1251, Malimpung mali1283, with Pattinjo as a western Enrekang dialect). All the Indonesian-language descriptions are titled 'bahasa Massenrempulu' and Glottolog files them under Duri [mvp]; Djunaidi 1993 is the one that separates the three dialects. The Grimes wordlist and areal note quoted here are specifically the Enrekang variety (list taken at Enrekang town).
